highlights.text: a root (aṣl) indicating dispersal and separation
jāʾa al-qawmu ashtātan: "the people came in scattered groups."
He cites al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "The clan's united body was scattered after it had been joined together
highlights.note: al-Ṭirimmāḥ, Umayyad; the entry names no earlier poet

highlights.text: a season of the year
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core meaning of the root

highlights.text: al-shitā' ("winter"), the opposite of al-ṣayf ("summer")
Ibn Fāris cites a line of Ṭarafah illustrating the word in use
al-shuwāẓ (الشُّوَاظ) is the pure flame-tip of a fire
he cites {shuwāẓun min nār}, "a shuwāẓ of fire" (Q 55:35, Sūrat al-Raḥmān)
highlights.note: شُوَاظ, 1 time: the entry's own Qur'anic attestation

highlights.text: a single underlying sense — "mixing" (al-khalṭ).
shubtu ash-shayʾa ashūbuhu shawban — "I mixed the thing / I mix it / a mixing."
highlights.note: شَوْب, 1 time: the verbal noun shawb, a mixing

highlights.text: roughness combined with a sharp point or tip on something.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's unifying idea for the root

highlights.text: al-Shawkah — derived abstractly from the same root: intensity or strength of military might/fighting power
Ibn Fāris treats ش-و-ر as two steady root-senses
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris gives the root two origins

highlights.text: Consultation belongs here: شَاوَرْتُ فلانًا في أمري ("I consulted so-and-so about my affair")
Hence the proverb he quotes: "Beware of public speeches — they are a show-ground with much stumbling."
al-amr al-hayyin — something easy, minor, or trifling.
al-shawā (a homonymous plural, of shawāh) — the scalp-skin
al-shawā also means the extremities/limbs
shawaytu al-laḥma / ishtawaytuhu — I roasted the meat
highlights.note: يَشْوِى, 1 time: to roast or scald

highlights.text: illustrated with two verses about roasting meat over a fire
highlights.note: unattributed verses; the entry names no poet, and they attest the roasting sense

highlights.text: one single idea — "elevation" or "rising up" in something (irtifāʿ fī shayʾ)
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single idea for the root

highlights.text: Shukhūṣ al-baṣar — the eyes becoming fixed and raised, staring without blinking
تأخرت عنه شيئاً ("I fell back from him a shayʾ") means "a little, slightly."
one says إذا شئت ("whenever you wish")
Zuhayr b. Masʿūd uses يا شيء ما as an exclamation of admiration
two distinct roots: (I) support and aid, and (II) spreading and diffusion
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris gives the root two separate origins

highlights.text: الشِّيعَة (al-shīʿa) — helpers and supporters.
شَاعَ الْحَدِيثُ (shāʿa al-ḥadīth) — a report spread, became widely known.
both turning on the idea of one thing being mixed into another
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's root sense, shared with sh-w-b

highlights.text: The core use is shayb, the greying of the head; the verb is shāba / yashību ("to go grey")
highlights.note: شَيْب, شَيْبَة: the greying of the head

highlights.text: mashīb is a man's crossing over into the class of the shīb — the aged, grey-haired men
On ʿAdī's line "and the head — greyness has shābahu it,"
highlights.note: ʿAdī, pre-Islamic; attests the greying sense

highlights.text: shāda al-ḥāʾiṭa yashīduhu shayḍan: "he plastered/coated a wall with al-shīd"
highlights.note: al-Zabīdī's core verb and the substance shīd

highlights.text: المشِيد (mashīd, pattern of amīr): "that which is worked/finished with al-shīd," i.e. plastered/coated.
Two Qur'anic citations anchor this sense: {وَقَصْرٍ مَّشِيدٍ} "a mashīd palace" (22:45) and {فِي بُرُوجٍ مُّشَيَّدَةٍ} "in mushayyada towers" (4:78)
المُشَيَّد (mushayyad, pattern of muʾayyad): according to Abū ʿUbayd, this means "the elongated/heightened building"
highlights.note: مُّشَيَّدَة, 1 time: a second reported sense

highlights.text: A line of poetry is quoted describing a structure plastered with marble and coated with lime
highlights.note: unattributed verse; the entry names no poet

highlights.text: A ḥadīth is cited: whoever exposes ("ashāda") a Muslim's faults without right will be disgraced by God
highlights.note: a hadith, used for the sense 'to expose publicly'

highlights.text: A *shaykh* is one in whom age has become visible and on whom grey hair has appeared
highlights.note: Ibn Manẓūr's core sense of the root

highlights.text: Ibn Manẓūr records disagreement on the threshold: from fifty onward; or from fifty-one to the end of life; or the span from fifty to eighty
attested in a verse of the pre-Islamic poet ʿAbīd ibn al-Abraṣ
Sībawayh treats one of its forms as poetic licence, comparing a line of Jadhīma al-Abraṣ
a single root whose core idea is **instability of movement** — a thing that does not travel in one fixed direction
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core idea for the root

highlights.text: the wolf is so called because of its تَذَؤُّب — its roving, coming at things from no single quarter
highlights.note: ذِّئْب, 3 times: why the wolf is so named

highlights.text: cites a line of verse (poet unnamed) as evidence: "Truly I, when a people's lion has taken flight
highlights.note: unattributed verse; the entry names no poet

highlights.text: dislike/aversion combined with fault
al-dhaʾm — fault, blemish; one so described is madhʾūm.
following along / compliance and submission
aḏʿana (Form IV) — "he complied/submitted" (yuḏʿinu, iḏʿānan = compliance)
highlights.note: مُذْعِنِين, 1 time: the Form IV verb

highlights.text: covering many distinct senses that share the consonant root but diverge widely in meaning
highlights.note: Ibn Manẓūr's senses diverge; no one shared meaning

highlights.text: الذَّبّ (al-dhabb) = to repel, ward off, or drive away.
highlights.note: the sense the entry traces مُّذَبْذَبِين back to

highlights.text: مُذَبْذِب/مُتَذَبْذِب = a man torn between two people or courses, settled with neither.
This is the sense used in the Qurʾān's description of the hypocrites
highlights.note: the entry on the Qur'an's own usage

highlights.text: A verse of Abū Dhuʾayb uses ذَبْذَبَا for "they kept [rivals] dangling/trailing behind."
highlights.note: Abū Dhuʾayb, lived into Islam; attests the dangling sense

highlights.text: which Ibn Manẓūr glosses as "driven off and repelled from both sides," tracing it to sense (1)
highlights.note: Ibn Manẓūr's own exegesis of Q 4:143

highlights.text: A ḥadīth about an unmarried man being "of the مُذَبذَبين" (driven off from both believers and monks) is read the same way
one underlying idea is splitting or cleaving open
الذَّبْح (dhabḥ) — the verbal noun of ذَبَحْتُ الشَّاةَ, "I slaughtered the sheep"
highlights.note: ذُبِحَ, يُذَبِّحُ: the act of slaughtering

highlights.text: الذِّبْح (dhibḥ, with kasra) — the passive sense: the thing slaughtered
having three separate root meanings: a small flying creature (the fly), to which other things are then compared; edge and sharpness; and agitation and movement
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris gives the doubled root three separate origins

highlights.text: al-dhubāb is the fly; one fly is dhubāba
the form in al-Nābigha's words "much given to striking at the flies with her lip"
highlights.note: al-Nābigha, pre-Islamic; attests the fly sense

highlights.text: beauty and freshness/bloom (ḥusn wa-naḍāra)
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core sense; he adds a separate root meaning 'to go away'

highlights.text: الذهب (al-ḏahab), the familiar metal
ذهاب الشيء (ḏahāb al-shayʾ), a thing's going or passing away
highlights.note: ذَهَبَ 35 times, ذَهَاب 1 time: to go, to pass away

highlights.text: verse of Qays comparing a faded encampment-trace
highlights.note: Qays, pre-Islamic; attests the gilded sense

highlights.text: being distracted or occupied away from something, whether by fright/terror (dhu'r)
dhahiltu 'ani sh-shay' ("I dhahal-ed from the thing") means you forgot it
derives ذ-ك-ر from two distinct roots.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris gives the root two separate origins

al-dhikr as verbal mention (remembrance "with the tongue")
highlights.note: ذِكْر, 76 times: mention with the tongue

highlights.text: a line of ʿAdī [b. Zayd] describing a powerful she-camel
highlights.note: ʿAdī b. Zayd, pre-Islamic; attests the maleness sense

highlights.text: whose meaning is sharpness and penetration in a thing
dhakkaytu l-dhabīḥa, "I slaughtered the animal", belongs to the same set of words
a single root meaning submission, humble yielding and softness

dābba dhalūl, a tractable, docile animal
"a little dhill (with i) better preserves family and wealth."
a single root (aṣl wāḥid) whose every use, he says, points to the opposite of praise
The person is then dhamīm or madhmūm, "blamed", meaning he is not praiseworthy.
A covenant (ʿahd) is called dhimām because a person is blamed for letting it be lost.
Dhū al-Rumma likens eyes to "the dhimām of wells that the water-drawers have drained"
highlights.note: Dhū al-Rumma, Umayyad; the entry names no earlier poet

highlights.text: Abū ʿUbayd glosses dhimma as a guarantee of safety (amān) in the Prophet's words wa-yasʿā bi-dhimmatihim
highlights.note: Abū ʿUbayd's gloss on a prophetic report

highlights.text: they are called ahl al-dhimma because they paid the jizya and so were made secure in their lives and property
In a ḥadīth a man asks the Prophet what will remove from him "the madhamma of suckling"
highlights.note: a hadith, for madhamma as a claim
